title: What amrit asks
hookLine: the five Ks, the daily banis and the four things avoided
carry: amrit's big yes lives in small daily keeps
tomorrow: prepare for months, or take it and grow? two Sikhs disagree.

lines: A NOTES PAGE: WHAT AMRIT ASKS.
A COMB. COTTON SHORTS. A BRACELET.
cards: The notes app on Simran's phone has a new page called what amrit asks. She expected the list to be dramatic: courage, devotion, giving your head. Then she copies out what the code actually says, and it's oddly small.
A comb. A pair of cotton shorts. A steel bracelet.
Prayers at dawn and at bedtime. A kind of meat not eaten. For the boldest picture in yesterday's lesson, why is the list so ordinary?

teach.h: THE FIVE Ks, KEPT ON THE BODY.
teach.b: Here's the list, from the Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, in three parts.
First, the five Ks, kept on the body: kesh, uncut hair; the kanga, a small wooden comb; the kara, a steel bracelet; the kachhera, cotton undershorts; and the kirpan, a sword kept sheathed.
Second, the daily banis, the Nitnem: set hymns at dawn, beginning with Japji, Rehras in the evening, and Sohila at night.
Third, the four kurahits, the things avoided: cutting the hair; eating kutha, meat killed the ritual way; sexual relations outside marriage; and tobacco. Now the puzzle.
Why is the head-on-your-palm step made of combs and morning prayers? Because a vow you feel once can fade. A vow you touch at the sink every morning is harder to lose.

teach.h: A BIG YES IN SMALL DAILY THINGS.
teach.b: The big yes gets broken into small things you'll meet every single day. And here's the surprise in Simran's list, the thing to tell a friend tonight. A Sikh who has never taken amrit may already keep some of it.
Simran's hair is uncut. She wears a kara.
She reads Japji on most mornings. Her list isn't a wall between her and amrit. It's a map, and it shows how far she's already walked.

how: At the amrit ceremony the five who give amrit explain the rehat aloud: the five Ks, the daily banis and the four things to avoid. Those who take amrit keep them every day.

s: amrit asks for one heroic feat, not ordinary habits
the code's list is daily: five Ks, set prayers, four things avoided.
tobacco is one of the four kurahits
with cutting the hair, eating kutha, and sexual relations outside marriage.
the five Ks are worn only on special days
they're kept on the body every day; that's where the vow lives.

games.q: Simran's cousin thinks taking amrit is one heroic moment, and then you're done. what does the Rehat Maryada's list show?
o: the vow is kept every day: five Ks on the body, the nitnem, four things avoided.
it's one ceremony; after that, nothing more is asked.
it asks only for courage in battle.
games.why: the head-on-the-palm yes is kept through a comb, a bracelet and morning prayers: small things met every single day.

practice: Count on your fingers, slowly, the things you already keep, not only religious ones: a habit you've held for years, a promise you haven't broken, a way you treat your family. One finger each.
Then rest your hands and notice how many are down.

wordCard.voice: What is asked. In the code: the five Ks, the daily banis, and four things avoided, all kept every day.
